The blade had a span of approximately 1.4 inches and a chord of 0.7 inches.
The blade was fabricated from two parts: an integrally cast base, airfoil suction surface, and cooling fins; and a formed sheet-metal pressure surface.
The gas-to-blade heat transfer coefficient was calculated using a correlation equation from previous research.
The blade-to-coolant heat transfer coefficient was calculated using two methods: one assuming fully developed flow, and one considering the length-to-diameter ratio of the coolant passage.
The calculated blade temperatures agreed within 3% at the midspan and tip regions compared to experimental data.
At the root region, the agreement was within 3% for turbulent flow and 10% for laminar flow.
The calculated cooling-air pressure losses agreed with experimental data within 5%.
The blade entrance loss coefficient determined experimentally was 0.37.
The entrance loss was 1-6% of the overall pressure loss for the range of cooling airflows tested.
The experimental cooling airflow rates ranged from 7x10^-4 to 8.6x10^-3 lb/s.
For the high-temperature turboprop conditions, the calculated blade temperatures agreed within 2% above midspan and 10% at 3/16 inch above the root compared to extrapolated experimental data.
The allowable blade temperature distribution was based on a stress ratio factor of 2.8 and 1000 hour life for the alloy 116-31.
The assumed turboprop engine had a compressor pressure ratio of 10.9, airflow of 13.4 lb/s, and turbine-inlet temperature of 2000°F.
The assumed flight condition was 300 knots at 30,000 ft altitude.
The shape of the effective gas temperature profile relative to the rotor blades was assumed similar to the experimental static cascade data.
